task_title: Effects of Human Behavior and Communication on the Learning Process
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how human behavior, needs, motivation, defense mechanisms and emotional reactions shape what a learner takes in, how adults learn, and how communication works and breaks down, and you can use that knowledge to adjust your ground and flight instruction for the person in front of you.
why: An effective instructor uses knowledge of human behavior, basic human needs, defense mechanisms and how adults learn to organize productive lessons [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. Technical knowledge is useless if the instructor fails to communicate it [[25:105|AIH 5-2]]. On the CFI checkride you will give examples, describe what you would do about abnormal behavior and defense mechanisms, and show that you communicate well on the ground and in the air.

warmup: Think first: your new learner, a 45-year-old business owner, shows up late, skipped the reading, and when you mention his rough landing last week he says the gusty wind made it impossible. He is pleasant, pays on time and says he really wants this certificate. What might be going on inside him, and what is the first thing you would say?

key_terms.def: How and why people function the way they do: a product of innate human nature plus individual experience and environment, and also the result of attempts to satisfy needs [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].
The reason a person acts or behaves a certain way. It lies at the heart of goals and is probably the dominant force in a learner's progress [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].
Maslow's 1954 model of human needs: physiological, safety and security, love and belonging, self-esteem and self-actualization [[25:38|AIH 2-5]] [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].
An unconscious mental process that protects a person from anxiety or unpleasant emotions. It often appears unconsciously and distorts reality [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].
Placing your own shortcomings or impulses onto someone else, like blaming a failed checkride on a "poor examiner" [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].
A subconscious way of justifying unacceptable actions with excuses the person sincerely believes [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].
A feeling of worry, nervousness or unease about something with an uncertain outcome. Probably the most significant psychological factor in flight instruction [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Short-term tiredness after long physical or mental strain, monotony or lack of sleep. Others see its signs before the person does [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].
A critical loss of water from the body. Its first noticeable effect is fatigue [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].
The three elements of communication: the sender, the codes used to send the message, and the listener or learner [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].
A general word that does not call up a specific mental image, like "aircraft." Overuse is a barrier to communication [[25:98|AIH 4-5]].
Stating your perception of the learner's behavior so the learner can confirm or clarify the feelings behind it [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

chunks.title: What human behavior is, and why a CFI studies it

body.p: Definitions of human behavior. The study of human behavior tries to explain how and why people function the way they do. Behavior comes from innate human nature plus each person's own experience and environment, and definitions vary by field of study [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. The AIH gives three ways to look at it:

head: Definition
What it says
Flight-training example
rows: Product of factors that cause predictable acts
Fear triggers innate responses like faster breathing, but how a person handles the fear comes from their own experience [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]
Two learners both fear steep turns. One avoids them; the other asks for extra ground review. Fear causes humans to fight or flee [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]
Result of attempts to satisfy needs
Needs can be simple, like food and water, or complex, like respect and acceptance [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]
A learner who wants the respect of coworkers may push for an early solo (see human needs below)
Typical life course
As a person matures, the mode of action moves from dependency to self-direction, so the learner's age affects how you design the curriculum [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]
Offer a curriculum that allows for each learner's tendency to self-direct [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]

body.p: Thoughts, feelings and behavior are shared by people to a large extent despite cultural differences [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. By watching behavior, you learn both about the learner's needs and about yourself as an instructor. Understanding human behavior leads to successful instruction [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].

Human nature and the two systems. Human nature is the set of psychological traits, feelings and behaviors all humans share [[25:41|AIH 2-8]]. Kahneman describes two systems that compete to control behavior: System 1 is fast, automatic, emotional and based on memory and experience; System 2 is slow, logical and takes conscious effort [[25:41|AIH 2-8]].

System 1 is lazy: it assumes a task is as simple as similar past tasks, which can lead to poor decisions. System 2 takes effort, so people slip back to System 1 as soon as the immediate problem is solved [[25:41|AIH 2-8]]. Knowing this helps you spot learner pitfalls such as treating a complex problem as a simple one, or reusing a recent solution on a task that only looks similar [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

callout.text: Application: when a learner answers a weather or fuel question instantly, ask "how do you know?" That pushes the thinking from System 1 into System 2, which the AIH says demands effort and self-control [[25:41|AIH 2-8]].

check.q: In the AIH, how does a learner's age affect your curriculum design?
check.a: As people mature their mode of action moves from dependency to self-direction, so the curriculum should allow for each learner's varying tendency to self-direct [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].

body.p: Instructor and learner relationship. Many educational psychologists believe everyone has a learning style tied to personality type, and that working with that style benefits both instructor and learner. The AIH notes the idea is controversial but widely used [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) of 1962 sorted behavior into sixteen types [[25:34|AIH 2-1]], and Keirsey condensed them into four groups: Guardian, Artisan, Rational and Idealist [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].

Personality type shapes how you teach as well as how the learner learns. Learners whose style matches the instructor's tend to retain information longer, apply it more effectively, learn more and like the course more. You cannot change your preferred style to match every learner, but you can take steps to bridge the gap [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].

The AIH example: Derek teaches with a clear, precise, step-by-step syllabus, much as he was taught. His learner Jason runs a wilderness adventure company and needs action and variety. Derek builds a scenario around scouting locations for future adventure tours, which pushes Derek out of his lock-step approach and ties the lesson to why Jason wants to fly [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].
Keeping the relationship healthy. Minimizing learner frustration is the instructor's responsibility [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. The AIH rules:

bullets: Motivate learners: show the benefit and purpose of each lesson [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Keep learners informed: tell them what is expected and what they can expect, post their progress and give notice of tests [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Approach learners as individuals, not as an average personality that fits no one [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Give credit when due, but praise given too freely becomes valueless [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Criticize constructively: name the error and how to fix it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Be consistent: if something is fine one day and wrong the next, the learner is confused [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].
Admit errors: bluffing destroys the learner's confidence in you [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

callout.text: The AIH warns that if an instructor does not "like" a learner, that subtle feeling may affect the instructor's ability to teach [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]. A learner's failure to perform often results from the instructor's inability to transfer the information [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

check.q: Your teaching style is step-by-step and your learner craves variety. What does the AIH say you can do?
check.a: You cannot change your preferred style, but you can bridge the difference [[25:35|AIH 2-2]], for example by building a scenario around the learner's own interests, as Derek did [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].

body.p: Motivation is the reason a person acts a certain way, and a goal is the object of the effort. Being smart or coordinated seldom guarantees success, but motivation routinely takes learners to the top, so part of your job is to discover what motivates each learner [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].

head: Kind
What it is
CFI use
rows: Positive
The promise or achievement of rewards: personal, social, financial, self-concept or public recognition [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]
Your default. Positive motivation is essential to true learning [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]
Negative
May engender fear; can help in certain situations but is less effective for learning [[25:35|AIH 2-2]]
Insecure, unpleasant training situations inhibit learning [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]
Intangible
Desire for personal comfort and security, group approval and a favorable self-image [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]
Show how the lesson makes flying safer and more comfortable; instructors often forget this one [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]
Tangible
A return for effort, such as financial gain, self-esteem or recognition, that should stay apparent during instruction [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]
Tie lessons whose payoff is not obvious to an operational need, ideally with a scenario [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]

body.p: Other motivators the AIH names: avoiding pain and injury, the attractive features of the skill, group approval, and a favorable self-image built from blocks of learning that each add insight and confidence [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]. Sources of motivation vary: fascination with flight, building abilities, self-image, family tradition, a career, prestige, fun or transportation. All of them offer some reward for hard work [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

Find out what motivates each learner. Ask "Why are you taking this course?" or "How do you plan to use what you learn?" in a short interview or information form [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. A short learner questionnaire or brief autobiography also shows their background and preferred learning styles [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

Keeping it up. Motivation cannot be transferred from one person to another [[25:37|AIH 2-4]], and it does not stay at one level: it can drop because of physical or mental disturbances or inadequate instruction [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. Reward success with positive feedback: praise incremental successes, relate daily accomplishments to lesson objectives and comment favorably on progress [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. Mark milestones against the ACS, then give the next challenge, such as doing the skill under pressure or while distracted [[25:37|AIH 2-4]] [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].
S1 examples, how behavior affects motivation and learning:

bullets: A learner told only "do it again" with no reason sees no tangible reward and learns less than one who can relate the objective to an operational need [[25:36|AIH 2-3]].
Unreasonable demands for performance and progress lower motivation; difficult but possible goals promote learning [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].
A learner who feels unsafe focuses on a "flee" response instead of the skill [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

callout.text: Application memory aid for the AIH's three positive-feedback habits: PRC. Praise incremental successes, Relate daily wins to objectives, Comment on progress [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].

check.q: A learner thinks the lesson on aircraft systems is a waste of time. Which kind of motivation is missing, and what is the AIH fix?
check.a: The tangible reward is not apparent. Make the learner aware of applications not immediately apparent and build scenarios that contain the elements to be practiced [[25:36|AIH 2-3]].

body.p: Human needs are things all people require for normal growth and development. Murray (1938) split them into primary, biological needs like food, and secondary, psychological needs like independence [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Maslow noticed some needs take precedence over others, for example thirst before hunger, and in 1954 published his hierarchy [[25:38|AIH 2-5]].

head: Need
What it is
What you do
rows: Physiological
Air, food, water and maintenance of the body. If a learner is unwell, little else matters [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]
Check that a learner is not hungry or tired before you teach [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]
Security (safety)
Keeping oneself from harm. A learner who does not feel safe cannot concentrate [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]
Stress flight safety and ease the learner into feared flight regions carefully [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]
Belonging
Overcoming loneliness and alienation. Learners are out of their normal surroundings, so the need is stronger [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Help new learners feel at ease and reinforce their decision to fly [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Esteem
Self-respect and respect from others, internal or external. Frustrated esteem leaves a person feeling inferior, weak, helpless and worthless [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Remember it may be the main reason the learner is in training [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Cognitive and aesthetic
Added later: the need to know and understand, with a dopamine "eureka" when something is learned, such as the first solo; and the emotional need of the artist [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Explain what is going on so the learner can make informed choices [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Self-actualization
Being and doing what the person was "born to do" [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]
Helping a learner reach full potential is the greatest challenge and reward of instructing [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]

body.p: What the AIH actually tells you to do. Later studies found the hierarchy is not universal and the order in which needs are met has little effect; the model has little empirical support [[25:38|AIH 2-5]]. Learners can fly a maneuver while hungry, so a need does not have to be met 100 percent [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. What matters is the focus of perception: verify that most needs are met (the law of readiness), then focus the learner's senses on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

callout.text: Do a pre-assessment before every lesson to confirm the learner is physically and mentally ready to learn [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Application: a two-minute chat on the ramp ("eaten? slept? anything on your mind?") covers several levels at once.

check.q: Does Maslow's order matter when you decide whether a learner is ready for today's lesson?
check.a: Not much. The AIH says the order has little to no effect on learning ability; verify that most needs have been met and then focus the learner's perception on the lesson [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

body.p: Defense mechanisms can be biological or psychological [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. The biological one is fight or flight: adrenaline, a fast heart rate and higher blood pressure. An anxious learner meeting impending and full stalls may go into fight or flight with little time to think, so take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage, then let the learner practice the stages in realistic scenarios until the comfort level grows [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

The psychological ego defense mechanism, from Freud (1894), is an unconscious process that protects a person from anxiety or unpleasant emotions. It softens feelings of failure and guilt and protects self-image [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. All of them share two properties: they often appear unconsciously, and they distort, transform or falsify reality [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

head: Mechanism
What it is
Aviation example
rows: Repression
Uncomfortable thoughts are pushed into inaccessible parts of the unconscious [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
A repressed fear of flying that blocks learning to fly [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
Denial
Refusing to accept a reality that is too threatening. Minimization is related: accepting it in a diluted form [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
After you find his water bottle under the rudder pedal, the solo learner denies being inattentive; minimizing, he admits it but says nothing bad happened [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
Compensation
Covering a perceived weakness by stressing strength in another area [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
Application: a learner weak on radio work keeps steering talk to his smooth landings
Projection
Placing your own shortcomings or impulses on someone else [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
"I failed because I had a poor examiner" [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
Rationalization
Sincerely believed, plausible excuses for unacceptable actions [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
"There was not enough time to learn it," while skipping the study group and practice quiz [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
Reaction formation
Faking a belief opposite to the true one because the true belief causes anxiety [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
A who-cares attitude covering loneliness and a hunger for acceptance [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
Fantasy
Daydreaming about how things should be instead of acting on how they are [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
A transitioning pilot dreams of the airline job instead of mastering the complex airplane [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
Displacement
Shifting an emotion from its real target to a safer substitute [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
Anger at the instructor over a grade aimed somewhere else [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]

body.p: Why they matter. Defense mechanisms relieve the symptoms, not the causes, and do not solve problems [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]. Most are normal, but excessive reliance usually follows a personal crisis such as a death in the family, a divorce or a failing grade. Watch for a change in personality, angry outbursts, depression, general lack of interest, drug or alcohol abuse, social withdrawal, preoccupation with certain ideas or an inability to concentrate [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].
S2b, what the instructor does about defense mechanisms:

bullets: Know the typical mechanisms and something about related behavior problems [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Use common sense and discuss the problem with the learner. The main objective is to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Remember the human psyche is fragile and inept measures can damage it. In severe cases with possible deep psychological problems, recommend a professional counselor [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Set difficult but possible goals in the lesson objectives and completion standards; unreasonable demands lower motivation [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

callout.text: Do not try to argue a learner out of a defense mechanism on the spot. It operates unconsciously and is not subject to normal conscious checks [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]; a calm private talk about the facts works better.

check.q: A learner who failed a stage check says the check instructor "had it in for him." Which mechanism, and what is your first step?
check.a: Projection, blaming someone else for his own shortcoming [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Use common sense and discuss it with him, aiming to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

chunks.title: Emotional reactions: anxiety, stress, impatience and worry

body.p: You do not need to be a psychologist, but you should analyze learner behavior before and during each lesson so you can choose how to teach what comes next [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

Anxiety and stress. Anxiety is probably the most significant psychological factor in flight instruction, because flying can feel threatening and the fear of falling is universal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Responses range from hesitating to act, to doing something even if it is wrong. Some people react better and faster under threat; many freeze; others act without rational thought [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Normal reactions tell you special instruction is needed to relieve the anxiety. Abnormal ones are even more important because they may signify a deep-seated problem [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

bullets: Treat fears as a normal reaction rather than ignoring them, and reinforce the learner's enjoyment of flying [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Introduce the maneuvers that cause anxiety with care, so the learner knows what to expect and what their reaction should be [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

Emphasize the benefits and pleasures of flying instead of constantly citing the unhappy results of poor performance, and present safe practices as the way to satisfying, uninterrupted flying, not only to prevent catastrophe [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

body.p: Stress is the body's response to physical and psychological demands, with adrenaline and higher heart rate, breathing and blood pressure [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Acute stress is short term and triggers fight or flight; chronic stress is an intolerable burden that exceeds the ability to cope and makes performance fall sharply. A pilot with chronic stress is not safe to exercise airman privileges [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Performance rises with stress, peaks, then falls off rapidly once stress exceeds the ability to cope; the key is to stop, think and analyze before jumping to a conclusion [[1:60|PHAK 2-21]].

Normal reactions to stress: the learner responds rapidly and exactly, within the limits of experience and training, thinks rationally, acts rapidly and is extremely sensitive to the surroundings. Many responses are automatic, which is why emergency training must come before a real emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

Impatience is a bigger deterrent to learning pilot skills than most people think: the learner wants an early solo or cross-country before the basics are learned [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Fix it by presenting preliminary training one step at a time with clear goals for each step, and naming the elements already mastered when you explain or demonstrate the next one [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. It can also come from instruction paced for a slow learner; advance a fast learner as soon as each goal is met, because disinterest grows quickly with unnecessary drill [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

Worry or lack of interest. Worried or upset learners are not ready to learn [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Worry may come from training progress or from life outside it, and the two cannot be separated. You are not responsible for outside troubles but cannot ignore them; key instruction to the interests the learner brings and divert attention from worries to the task [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Worries caused by the course itself are often due to course or instructor shortcomings, and the best cure is prevention: make sure learners know the objective of each step and, after each lesson, exactly how they are doing and what deficiencies remain [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

callout.text: Discouragement and emotional upsets are rare when learners feel nothing is being withheld from them or neglected in their training [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Close every lesson with an honest "here is where you are."

check.q: Your fast learner gets restless after you assign a third lesson of the same pattern work she already flies well. What emotional reaction is this, and what does the AIH say to do?
check.a: Impatience caused by instruction keyed to a slower pace. Advance her to the next step as soon as each goal is met; unnecessary repetition breeds disinterest [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

chunks.title: Discomfort, illness, fatigue, dehydration, and apathy from poor instruction

body.p: Physical discomfort, illness, fatigue and dehydration all slow learning in the classroom and in the airplane [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]:

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Physical discomfort
Attention pulled away by temperature extremes, poor ventilation, poor lighting, or noise and confusion; no normal learning rate however hard the learner tries [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Fix the environment first. Application: a seat cushion or open vent can matter more than another explanation
Illness
A cold or worse dulls vision, hearing and feeling, all essential to performance [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Postpone the lesson until the learner is over the illness [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Airsickness
A learner with even incipient airsickness cannot learn at a normal rate [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
End the flight as soon as it starts and lengthen flights as immunity builds. Keep the learner flying the controls, use fresh air, and avoid rough air and abrupt maneuvers [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Acute fatigue
Inattention, distractibility, errors in timing, neglect of secondary tasks, loss of accuracy and control, unawareness of building errors, irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Give a break; fatigue is the primary consideration in the length and frequency of lessons [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Chronic fatigue
Not enough recovery between episodes of acute fatigue; it mixes physiological and psychological causes, so rest alone may not fix it [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Judgment can become impaired; the underlying problem has to be solved [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Dehydration
Lower alertness and slower decisions; first effect is fatigue, then dizziness, weakness, nausea, tingling, cramps and extreme thirst [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Carry water and drink at frequent intervals on long flights whether thirsty or not; ventilate the cabin [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]

body.p: Fatigue is one of the most treacherous hazards because the pilot may not notice it until serious errors are made [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Complex operations bring it on faster than simple ones [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. The PHAK adds that rest and 8 hours of sound sleep ordinarily cure acute fatigue, and if you are suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

Dehydration numbers. The PHAK suggests two to four quarts of water every 24 hours as a guide; eight 8-ounce glasses make 64 ounces, or two quarts. Most people feel thirsty only at a 1.5-quart deficit or a loss of 2 percent of body weight, and the thirst mechanism arrives too late and turns off too easily [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. Hot flight decks, wind, humidity and diuretic drinks such as coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated sodas all add to it [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. Heatstroke, the body's inability to control its temperature, may only be recognized at a sudden collapse [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

Apathy due to inadequate instruction. Learners lose interest when they see the instructor has not prepared, or when instruction seems deficient, contradictory or insincere. Even an inexperienced learner notices right away [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Poor preparation leads to spotty coverage, misplaced emphasis, unnecessary repetition and a lack of confidence in the learner; always have a plan [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Pitch the lesson to the learner's level, and avoid distracting mannerisms, untidiness, irritation and talking down, which lose confidence that is hard to regain [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

callout.text: Use the IMSAFE checklist (Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion) as part of your pre-lesson check, and teach the learner to use it on themselves [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

check.q: Halfway through a hot summer lesson your learner is irritable and starts missing the radio calls he usually makes. Which two K2d conditions should you suspect, and what do you do?
check.a: Acute fatigue (irritability, neglect of secondary tasks) [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] and dehydration, whose first noticeable effect is fatigue [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Give a break or end the lesson, and get water into him [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

body.p: Some people react to stress abnormally: the response may be absent or inadequate, random or illogical, or more than the situation calls for [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. During flight training, you are usually the only one who sees the learner under pressure, so you are the one able to tell safe from unsafe piloting actions and to notice possible psychological problems [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
Signs of abnormal reactions to stress. None is an absolute indication, but any of them under stress calls for careful instructor evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]:

bullets: Inappropriate reactions: extreme over-cooperation, painstaking self-control, inappropriate laughter or singing, very rapid changes in emotion [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
Marked changes in mood on different lessons, such as excellent morale followed by deep depression [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].
Severe anger directed at the flight instructor, service personnel and others [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

body.p: S2a, serious abnormal emotional behavior: what the instructor does. An instructor who believes a learner may have a serious psychological abnormality must refrain from instructing that learner and is personally responsible for making sure the person does not continue training or become certificated [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]:

head: Step
Action
rows: 1. Get an unbiased look
Arrange for another instructor who does not know the learner to fly an evaluation flight [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]
2. Confer
The two instructors confer to decide whether further investigation or action is justified [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]
3. Use your legal lever

Your primary legal responsibility is the decision to endorse solo or recommend the practical test. If the concern stands after consulting the unbiased instructor, withhold those endorsements and recommendations [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]
4. Point to help
In severe cases, recommend the services of a professional counselor [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]

body.p: Look at yourself too. In difficult situations, examine both the learner's responses and your own responses to the learner; behavior may be a normal product of a complex learning situation or a sign of something hazardous [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Instructors meeting new technology face stress too, and how you handle it frames how your learners respond for years [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

callout.text: Do not diagnose. The AIH says you are not required to be a psychologist [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]; your job is to observe, get an unbiased second opinion, protect safety and withhold endorsements when warranted [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

check.q: After consulting an instructor who flew an unbiased evaluation, you both still believe your learner may have a serious psychological deficiency. What do you do with his solo endorsement?
check.a: Withhold it, along with any practical test recommendation [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

body.p: Teaching the adult learner. The AIH puts the average aviation learner at 30 years old, so instructors need to know the needs of adults. Dr. Malcolm Knowles founded the field of adult education in the late twentieth century [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]. Adults as learners [[25:50|AIH 2-17]] [[25:51|AIH 2-18]]:

bullets: Learn because they have a use for the knowledge or skill; learning is a means to an end [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Seek learning to cope with life-changing events such as marriage, divorce or a new job, and are ready to learn when they take on new roles [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Are autonomous and self-directed and need to exercise control [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Draw on a reservoir of life experience and knowledge [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Are goal oriented, relevancy oriented and practical, wanting immediate application [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Need respect; keeping or raising self-esteem is a strong secondary motivator [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].
Want to solve problems and use new knowledge right away [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

body.p: What the instructor does with adults [[25:50|AIH 2-17]] [[25:51|AIH 2-18]]:

head: Instructor action
Why
rows: Give a syllabus with clearly defined objectives
Shows how the training reaches the learner's own goals [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Integrate new ideas with what they already know
So they keep and use the new information [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Clarify expectations early; own only your own
You are responsible for your expectations, not the learner's [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Let them control pace and start and stop time
Adults need control [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Use frequent scenario-based training
Fits the preference to self-direct and self-design learning [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Remember self-direction is not isolation
Self-directed projects still use other people as resources and guides [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
Use books, programmed instruction and computers
Popular with adults [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]
No spoon-feeding; set a cooperative climate; plan together
Adults want learning that is problem oriented and personalized [[25:51|AIH 2-18]]

body.p: Adults also bring life circumstances: financial stress or security, and age-related problems such as diminished hearing or eyesight [[25:51|AIH 2-18]]. Aviation instructors have an advantage, since the typical aviation learner is an adult willing to spend time and money, with more motivation, prior knowledge and decision-making skill than a typical school learner [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

callout.text: Application: with an adult, start a new topic by asking what they already know about it from work or life, then build on it. That uses their reservoir of experience [[25:50|AIH 2-17]] and the AIH advice to integrate new ideas with old [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

check.q: Name two things the AIH tells you to do because adults are self-directed.
check.a: Recognize their need to control pace and start and stop time, and give frequent SBT opportunities; also create chances for mutual planning [[25:50|AIH 2-17]] [[25:51|AIH 2-18]].

body.p: Communication happens when one person transmits ideas or feelings to another, and its effectiveness is measured by how similar the idea received is to the idea sent [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. You have communicated well when the learner understood the idea the way you intended [[25:94|AIH 4-1]].
Basic elements of communication. There are three, and each depends on the others [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]:

head: Element
What it is
What makes it work
rows: Source
Sender, speaker, writer, encoder, transmitter or instructor [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]

Three factors: choose language the receiver understands (no "ILS, TCAS, TAWS" with a new learner); reveal confidence and that the message matters; use accurate, up-to-date, stimulating material, since out-of-date information costs credibility [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Symbols
Simple oral, visual or tactile codes: words, gestures, facial expressions [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Combine them into meaningful wholes. Use several channels, visual, auditory and kinesthetic: move the trim wheel while the learner holds the attitude so she feels what trim does [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]
Receiver
Listener, reader, decoder or learner [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]

Know three characteristics: abilities, attitudes and experiences [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. Communication succeeds only when the receiver reacts with understanding and changes behavior as intended [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]

body.p: Feedback runs both ways. Monitor feedback from the learner to catch misunderstandings, for example by asking the learner to explain new information while you present it, then change your symbols as needed [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]. In Figure 4-2 the learner hears "stalls" and thinks of the engine quitting; the instructor catches it from the reply and clarifies [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

Learners need feedback from you too. Praise builds self-confidence and reinforces good behavior. Give negative feedback only in private, as a nonjudgmental description of the actual performance: say a safety wire job is not satisfactory, not that it is careless [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

About the receiver: judge the learner's background and familiarity with aviation, but do not assume. A college degree does not guarantee rapid progress; base your style on what the learner knows about the aviation subject [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. Attitudes may show resistance, willingness or passive neutrality, so use a varied approach [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

callout.text: S-S-R: Source, Symbols, Receiver. The AIH chapter summary calls awareness of these three the foundation of a successful communicator [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

check.q: You tell a new learner to "trim it out" and nothing happens. Using the elements of communication, what do you change?
check.a: Change the symbols and channels: let her feel the control pressure change while you move the trim wheel, explaining what she feels, so "trim" gains meaning [[25:95|AIH 4-2]]. Then check her understanding through feedback [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

body.p: Barriers to effective communication. The way language is used often causes misunderstandings, and the AIH names four barriers: lack of common experience, confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object, overuse of abstractions, and external factors [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

head: Barrier
What happens
Fix
rows: Lack of common experience
Probably the greatest single barrier. Words do not carry meaning like a truck carries bricks; they only stir a response based on the learner's own experience [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]
Speak the learner's language and spend time making sure needed terms are understood [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. "Time the magnetos" is not about a stopwatch [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]
Confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object
A word is confused with what it stands for, like "mechanic" for an AMT [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]
Allow for misreading and pick words that say what you mean [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]
Overuse of abstractions
General words like "aircraft" or "engine" call up different pictures in each mind [[25:98|AIH 4-5]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Use concrete words: "go around," not "take appropriate measures" [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
External factors
Outside the instructor's control: physiological (hearing loss, illness, multitasking), environmental (cabin noise) and psychological (fear, mistrust, low commitment) [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Mitigate: postpone for illness, a seat cushion, headsets and intercom or earplugs, and build trust [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]

body.p: Interference. The message gets disrupted, cut short or added to somewhere along the way, while both people believe it arrived intact. Noise and psychological factors cause it. Confirm the message by watching its effect, and use more feedback and confirmation [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

Multitasking as a barrier. People can handle two simple, low-level tasks at once, but a higher-level task needs full concentration, and adding even a simple activity reduces comprehension and recall of both [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. Application: do not brief a new concept while the learner is taxiing in a busy ramp.

English as a second language. Note whether it creates a significant barrier [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]. To be eligible for a student pilot certificate an applicant must be able to read, speak, write and understand English, with medical exceptions handled by operating limitations [[60:270|14 CFR 61.83]]. Flight and ground instructors are responsible for making sure those they train continuously meet the FAA Aviation English Language Standard [[10:3|AC 60-28B para 5.1]].

callout.text: R2 risk: a learner who nods but has decoded your words differently will act on the wrong picture in flight. Words in themselves transfer no meaning [[25:97|AIH 4-4]], so always confirm with a learner response, not a nod.

check.q: On a bad approach you call "take appropriate measures" and the learner keeps descending. Which barrier is this and what should you have said?
check.a: Overuse of abstractions. Say "go around," a concrete action with the same meaning to both of you [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

body.p: Developing communication skills. They do not happen automatically; they come from experience that begins with role playing in instructor training, continues while instructing and grows with more training [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

head: Skill
What the AIH says
How you use it
rows: Role playing
The learner gets a general situation and applies a new skill in a role. A flight instructor plays the learner pilot, copies known learner responses, then critiques you [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]

Practice in a nonthreatening setting where it is easier to find a comfortable style [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. In the AIH example, Ray plays an anxious learner during stalls while James briefs, demonstrates and talks him through [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
Instructional communication
Instruction has happened when you explain a procedure and then see the desired response [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
Teach what you know well; use your own experiences to illustrate but avoid "there I was" war stories; check whether performance was retained or a one-time event; teach how and why [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]
Listening
Know your learners by listening well, and self-evaluate [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. Listening is "hearing with comprehension" [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]
Use the listening tools in Figure 4-5 and teach learners to listen (Figure 4-6) [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]
Questioning
Shows how well the learner understands and that you are paying attention [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Ask focused, open-ended "why" and "how" questions; avoid closed-ended ones that test only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Instructional enhancement
The more you know about a subject, the better you convey it; you never stop learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Be ready to answer beyond the lesson, but present only what fits the learner's level [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]

body.p: Teaching learners to listen. Wanting to listen is one technique; others are listening for main ideas ("what is the purpose of what I am listening to?"), guarding against daydreaming by repeating, paraphrasing or summarizing in the spare time a fast listener has, and taking notes in their own shorthand rather than word for word [[25:101|AIH 4-8]] [[25:102|AIH 4-9]]. Remind learners that emotions interfere: a learner terrified of spins may not be able to listen to a spin lesson until the fear is eased [[25:101|AIH 4-8]].

Good questions. Adapt each question to the learner's ability, experience and stage of training, keep it to one idea (who, what, when, where, why or how, not a mix), and make it a challenge of suitable difficulty [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Confirm understanding with paraphrasing (say what the learner's statement meant to you) and perception checking (say what you perceive about the learner's feelings so they can clarify) [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. Phrase questions to focus the learner on decision-making and judgment [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

callout.text: In the airplane: brief the maneuver on the ground with a model or sketch, keep in-flight words short and concrete, and debrief with open "how" and "why" questions. The flight instructor has to develop good ground instruction skills to prepare learners for what happens in the air [[25:100|AIH 4-7]].

check.q: Rewrite "Did you understand the crosswind correction?" as a better question.
check.a: Make it open-ended and focused, for example "How would you set the controls for a left crosswind on this runway?" Closed yes/no questions test only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

chunks.title: Risks: misreading behavior and communication breakdowns

body.p: Recognizing and accommodating human behavior (R1). The hazard is teaching a learner whose needs, emotions or defenses block perception. Hungry, tired or frightened learners focus on the need, not on you [[25:38|AIH 2-5]], and an anxious learner may freeze or act without thinking [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Learners who think their instruction is inadequate or your demands unreasonable lose motivation however keen they are [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

head: Risk
How you spot it
How you accommodate
rows: Unmet needs
The pre-assessment shows the learner is not physically or mentally ready [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]
Verify most needs are met before teaching [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Application: if they are not, change or delay the lesson
Fear of a flight region
Hesitancy, freezing or rash inputs [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Ease into it carefully, describe what to expect, take the maneuver apart into stages [[25:39|AIH 2-6]] [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
Defense mechanisms hiding a real problem
Excuses, blame, denial; personality change after a crisis [[25:43|AIH 2-10]] [[25:44|AIH 2-11]]
Private talk to restore motivation and confidence; counselor in severe cases [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Physiological obstacles
Unfamiliar noise, vibration, G-forces, stomach discomfort [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]
Explain the causes; never ridicule a learner who is affected [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]

body.p: Barriers to communication (R2). The hazard is a message that both people think was received intact but was not [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. In the air, noise, workload and fear stack up. Mitigate with headsets and intercom [[25:99|AIH 4-6]], concrete terms [[25:99|AIH 4-6]], one idea per question [[25:103|AIH 4-10]], and confirmation by watching the effect of the message [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

callout.text: Mistrust or fear between instructor and learner disrupts communication and severely inhibits the flow of information [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. A frightening first lesson, such as stalls on day one, can make a new learner wonder if flying is a good idea; introduce emergencies after normal operations are familiar [[25:161|AIH 8-3]].

check.q: Why is "the learner said yes, he understood" not enough to manage the communication risk?
check.a: Interference can distort a message while both sides think it arrived intact; confirm it by observing the effect of the message and with more feedback [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

body.p: These are instructor errors the AIH warns about in this Task. Each one is easy to commit and easy to be asked about.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Assuming all learners are alike
Lessons aimed at an average personality that fits no one [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]
Find each learner's goals with an interview or questionnaire [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]
Relying on negative motivation
An insecure learner who learns less [[25:36|AIH 2-3]]
Use positive motivation and reward incremental success [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]
Ignoring a learner's fear
Freezing, hesitancy or impulsive inputs [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Treat fears as normal; explain what to expect before the maneuver [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Holding a fast learner back
Impatience, then disinterest [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Advance as soon as each goal is met [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Teaching an unprepared lesson
Apathy and lost confidence [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Always have a plan [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]
Talking down or criticizing in public
Lost confidence that is hard to regain [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]
Negative feedback only in private, describing performance without judgment [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]
Arguing with a defense mechanism
More excuses and blame [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]
Discuss calmly; aim to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Jargon and abstractions
Nods without understanding [[25:95|AIH 4-2]] [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]
Concrete terms and a learner explanation back to you [[25:99|AIH 4-6]] [[25:96|AIH 4-3]]
Closed or multi-part questions
Yes/no answers that show only rote learning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Focused, open-ended, one idea per question [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]
Flying on with a fatigued or airsick learner
Timing errors, irritability, nausea [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Take a break or end the flight [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]

callout.text: On the checkride, narrate your reasoning: "I am asking an open-ended question here because closed-ended ones only check rote learning" [[25:103|AIH 4-10]]. The examiner wants to hear the AIH behind your choices.

check.q: Your learner made a sloppy safety-related mistake on the ramp in front of other learners. How do you give the feedback?
check.a: In private, as a nonjudgmental description of what actually happened, not a label like "careless" [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

scenario.title: The learner who blames the wind
scenario.setup: Marcus is a 45-year-old restaurant owner with 22 hours. He wants to fly to his second restaurant two hours away. He arrives ten minutes late from a lunch rush, has not eaten, and the ramp is 95 degrees. His last landings were rough and he says the gusty wind made them impossible, though the winds were light. He is pushing to solo next week and keeps asking why he has to do more ground work on "boring" systems. During the last flight, when you told him to "fix the approach," he added power and kept descending.

questions.q: Before you go near the airplane, what do you check and why?
questions.a: His readiness to learn: hunger, heat and rushing are needs and discomforts that pull his focus off the lesson. Do a pre-assessment that he is physically and mentally ready [[25:39|AIH 2-6]], and watch for dehydration and fatigue in the heat [[25:47|AIH 2-14]] [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

questions.q: What is his comment about the wind most likely to be, and how do you respond?
questions.a: A defense mechanism, likely rationalization (a sincerely believed excuse) [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Do not argue; discuss it calmly using the facts, aiming to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

questions.q: How do you handle his push to solo next week?
questions.a: It is impatience: seeking the final objective without the preliminary training. Present the training one step at a time with clearly stated goals for each step [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

questions.q: How do you make the systems lessons matter to him as an adult learner?
questions.a: Adults learn because they have a use for the knowledge [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]. Tie each systems topic to his goal, the trip to his second restaurant, and build a scenario around it so the tangible reward is apparent [[25:36|AIH 2-3]].

questions.q: What went wrong with "fix the approach," and what do you say next time?
questions.a: Overuse of abstractions: the words did not call up the action you meant [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]. Use concrete terms, such as "go around" or a specific pitch and power instruction [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

questions.q: How do you confirm he really understood today's briefing?
questions.a: Ask focused, open-ended "how" and "why" questions and have him explain the plan back; use paraphrasing to check meaning [[25:103|AIH 4-10]] [[25:96|AIH 4-3]].

skills.do: Give examples of how human behavior affects motivation and learning (ACS FI.I.A.S1). The examiner hears you link specific behavior to motivation and learning, for example how an unmet need, a fear or an unseen reward changes what a learner takes in, with what you would do about it.
skills.practice: Write one airplane example for each motivation type (positive, negative, tangible, intangible) [[25:35|AIH 2-2]] [[25:36|AIH 2-3]] and for each Maslow level [[25:39|AIH 2-6]] [[25:40|AIH 2-7]]. Say them out loud in under a minute each.

skills.do: Describe what the instructor can do to deal with: a. serious abnormal emotional behavior, and b. defense mechanisms (ACS FI.I.A.S2). The examiner expects the evaluation flight by an unacquainted instructor, conferring, and withholding endorsements for (a), and naming the mechanism, a calm private discussion, restoring motivation and self-confidence, and counselor referral in severe cases for (b).
skills.practice: Memorize the three abnormal-stress signs [[25:48|AIH 2-15]] and the two steps for a suspected serious abnormality [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]. For each of the eight defense mechanisms, write a learner quote and your response [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] [[25:43|AIH 2-10]] [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

skills.do: Use effective communication in ground and flight instruction (ACS FI.I.A.S3). The examiner watches you brief and teach: concrete words, several channels, open-ended questions, active listening, checking understanding, and private, nonjudgmental correction.
skills.practice: Role-play with a CFI playing a confused or anxious learner, as the AIH describes [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. Record a ground briefing and count your closed-ended questions and abstractions, then redo it [[25:103|AIH 4-10]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the AIH's ways of defining human behavior?
options: A product of factors that cause people to act in predictable ways
A fixed set of traits that training cannot change
A focus on the typical life course of humans
The result of attempts to satisfy certain needs
quiz.why: The AIH gives the predictable-factors view, the needs view and the life-course view [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].

quiz.q: Keirsey condensed the sixteen MBTI types into which four groups?
options: Visual, Auditory, Kinesthetic, Reading
Guardian, Artisan, Rational, Idealist
Leader, Follower, Thinker, Doer
Rote, Understanding, Application, Correlation
quiz.why: Keirsey's four groups are Guardian, Artisan, Rational and Idealist [[25:35|AIH 2-2]].

quiz.q: Learners seeking intangible rewards are motivated by personal comfort and security, group approval and what else?
options: Financial gain
Public recognition
A favorable self-image
A pilot certificate
quiz.why: The intangible motivators are comfort and security, group approval and a favorable self-image [[25:36|AIH 2-3]].

quiz.q: A learner answers your fuel question instantly, using the burn from a similar flight last week, and gets it wrong. In Kahneman's two-system model in the AIH, what happened?
options: System 1 assumed the task was as simple as a similar past one
System 2 took over, and slow, rigid logic produced the wrong figure
System 2 was overloaded, so his memory of the past flight failed him
System 1 is the slow, logical system, so he needed more time to finish
quiz.why: System 1 is fast, automatic and based on memory and experience. Because it is lazy, it assumes a task is as simple as similar past tasks, which can lead to poor decisions. System 2 is the slow, logical system that takes conscious effort [[25:41|AIH 2-8]].

quiz.q: Which two defense mechanisms does the AIH call primary?
options: Repression and denial
Projection and fantasy
Compensation and displacement
Rationalization and reaction formation
quiz.why: Repression and denial are the two primary defense mechanisms [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

quiz.q: A learner covers loneliness and a hunger for acceptance with a who-cares attitude. Which mechanism is this?
options: Displacement
Reaction formation
Compensation
Fantasy
quiz.why: Reaction formation is faking a belief opposite to the true one [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

quiz.q: Which is listed as a sign of acute fatigue?
options: Over-cooperation
Improved accuracy
Extreme thirst
Neglect of secondary tasks
quiz.why: The AIH list includes neglect of secondary tasks along with inattention, timing errors and irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH say is the first noticeable effect of dehydration?
options: Fatigue
Abdominal cramps
Tingling of hands and feet
Dizziness
quiz.why: The first noticeable effect of dehydration is fatigue [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

quiz.q: What are the three basic elements of communication?
options: Speaker, message, noise
Encoder, channel, feedback
Source, symbols, receiver
Instructor, lesson, critique

quiz.q: Which barrier does the AIH call probably the greatest single barrier to effective communication?
options: External factors
Overuse of abstractions
Confusion between the symbol and the symbolized object
Lack of common experience
quiz.why: Lack of common experience is probably the greatest single barrier [[25:97|AIH 4-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is hungry and tired but insists on flying today. What does the AIH guidance support?
options: Fly the full lesson, since needs do not have to be met before learning
Delay the lesson until every Maslow level is fully met
Pre-assess him and teach only if he is physically and mentally ready
Fly the lesson but skip the debrief to save his energy
final_quiz.why: A thorough pre-assessment should verify the learner is physically and mentally ready to learn [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]; a hungry or tired learner may not perform as expected [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says she failed her written test only because she had a cold that week, though she skipped every practice test you assigned. She sincerely believes it. Which mechanism fits best?
options: Projection
Fantasy
Rationalization
Repression
final_quiz.why: Rationalization: plausible excuses the person sincerely believes, without admitting skipped study [[25:43|AIH 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: Over three lessons a learner swings from excellent morale to deep depression, and on the third flight laughs loudly during a near stall. What is your next step?
options: Ignore it; mood swings and laughter are normal reactions to training stress
Tell him to see a psychologist, and keep flying the syllabus meanwhile
Endorse him for solo so the responsibility builds his confidence
Have an unacquainted instructor fly an evaluation flight, then confer
final_quiz.why: Marked mood changes and inappropriate laughter under stress call for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]; have an unacquainted instructor fly an evaluation and confer [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your transition learner keeps talking about his future airline job but makes no progress on the complex airplane. Which defense mechanism is the AIH example?
options: Displacement
Fantasy
Compensation
Denial
final_quiz.why: Fantasy: daydreaming about the airline career instead of working toward the certification [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is angry about a stage check grade and snaps at the line service staff instead of you. What is this?
options: Displacement
Projection
Reaction formation
Minimization
final_quiz.why: Displacement shifts the emotion to a less threatening target [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

final_quiz.q: Before her first lesson on spins your learner is visibly terrified. What does the AIH say about listening in this state?
options: Fear sharpens her listening, so give the full spin briefing right now
Ask only closed-ended questions, since open ones would add to her fear
Have her take verbatim notes so the fear cannot make her miss anything
Her emotions may overwhelm her listening, so allay the fear first
final_quiz.why: Emotions interfere with listening; a learner terrified of spins may be overwhelmed, which requires a means to allay the anxiety [[25:101|AIH 4-8]].

final_quiz.q: In a hot, noisy trainer without an intercom, which accommodation does the AIH suggest for the noise?
options: Speak louder and repeat each instruction twice
Hand signals only
Earplugs, which also clarify speaker output
Brief everything in flight
final_quiz.why: If no intercom is available, earplugs are a good solution and actually clarify speaker output [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

final_quiz.q: A learner who is a skilled A&P mechanic gets the same beginner preflight briefing as everyone else and tunes out. What went wrong?
options: You did not adjust the briefing to his level
Nothing; every learner must get an identical briefing
He is using a defense mechanism to avoid the lesson
He is showing acute fatigue from a long workday
final_quiz.why: Instruction should be presented differently for a skilled AMT than for someone with no experience; teach for the level of the learner [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

final_quiz.q: Your ground lesson on airspace uses a handout from rules that have since changed, and a sharp learner notices. Which source factor of communication did you miss, and what does it cost you?
options: Using accurate, up-to-date material; out-of-date facts cost credibility
Showing confidence in the message; it makes the topic seem unimportant
Choosing words the learner knows; it leaves her confused by the acronyms
Getting feedback from the receiver; it hides whether she understood you
final_quiz.why: The AIH gives three factors for the source: selecting language the receiver understands, revealing confidence that the message matters, and speaking from accurate, up-to-date and stimulating material. Out-of-date information causes the instructor to lose credibility [[25:95|AIH 4-2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says "I think I get it." You respond, "So you are saying the trim takes away the pressure you have to hold, right?" What technique is this?
options: Perception checking
Paraphrasing
Role playing
Closed-ended questioning
final_quiz.why: Paraphrasing shows what the learner's statement meant to you so she can correct or expand it [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: You pull the throttle for a simulated engine failure, and your well-trained learner pitches for best glide and picks a field almost without thinking. What does the AIH say about this normal reaction to stress?
options: It is abnormal, since a normal learner would freeze until told what to do
It shows a lack of anxiety, so the scenario was not realistic enough to count
Normal; many stress responses are automatic, so train emergencies first
It is a defense mechanism, since acting fast hides her fear of the failure
final_quiz.why: Under stress, normal individuals respond rapidly and exactly within the limits of their experience and training. Many responses are automatic, which highlights the need for proper training in emergency operations before an actual emergency [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. Freezing is one possible response to anxiety, not the normal reaction described here [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner gets quiet and tense whenever you begin steep turns, but she flies them correctly and shows no other unusual behavior. Why does the AIH say this normal anxiety reaction still matters to you?
options: It does not; only abnormal reactions are of concern to an instructor
It means steep turns should come out of her syllabus for a while
It means she may have a deep-seated psychological problem to refer
It signals a need for special instruction to relieve the anxiety
final_quiz.why: Both normal and abnormal reactions to anxiety concern the flight instructor. Normal reactions are significant because they indicate a need for special instruction to relieve the anxiety; abnormal reactions are even more important because they may signify a deep-seated problem. Anxiety is countered by treating fears as normal and introducing the maneuvers with care, not by dropping them [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: A learner pilot's English is hard for ATC to understand. Who is responsible for monitoring that learners in training meet the FAA English standard?
options: Only the examiner at the practical test
Flight and ground instructors, among others
Only ATC
No one until the commercial certificate
final_quiz.why: Flight and ground instructors are among those responsible for making sure people in training continuously meet the FAA Aviation English Language Standard [[10:3|AC 60-28B para 5.1]].

takeaways: Behavior comes from human nature plus each person's experience, and from trying to meet needs [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].
Find out what motivates each learner and keep the reward visible; use positive motivation [[25:35|AIH 2-2]] [[25:36|AIH 2-3]].
Check that most needs are met before teaching; the order of Maslow's levels matters little [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].
Defense mechanisms treat symptoms, not causes; respond with a calm talk aimed at restoring motivation and confidence [[25:44|AIH 2-11]] [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Seriously abnormal behavior: an unbiased evaluation flight, confer, and withhold endorsements [[25:49|AIH 2-16]].
Adults want relevance, control and respect; give them objectives, SBT and mutual planning [[25:50|AIH 2-17]] [[25:51|AIH 2-18]].
Communication is two-way: concrete words, several channels, open-ended questions and confirmation by the learner's response [[25:95|AIH 4-2]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]] [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].
cfi_notes: Expect the examiner to give you a learner quote and ask which defense mechanism it shows. Have one aviation example ready for each of the eight [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] [[25:43|AIH 2-10]] [[25:44|AIH 2-11]].

The AIH gives different average ages: the Figure 2-1 caption says the average learner pilot is 34 and the average maintenance learner 25 [[25:35|AIH 2-2]], while the adult learner section says the average aviation learner is 30 [[25:50|AIH 2-17]]. The 30 may cover pilots and maintenance learners together, but the AIH does not say. Either way, plan for adult learners.

The AIH disagrees with itself on the barriers: the text lists four barriers ending with external factors and treats interference as its own topic [[25:97|AIH 4-4]] [[25:99|AIH 4-6]], but Figure 4-3 labels the four hurdles interference, abstractions, symbol confusion and lack of common experience [[25:97|AIH 4-4]]. Teach the four from the text and mention interference too.

The AIH presents Maslow's pyramid and then says the hierarchy has little empirical support and the order matters little [[25:38|AIH 2-5]] [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. On the checkride, show you know the levels and the AIH's conclusion: verify most needs are met.
The AIH points to "AC 60-28" for English language questions [[25:98|AIH 4-5]]; the current version in our sources is AC 60-28B, which cancels 60-28A [[10:1|AC 60-28B para 2]].
The RMH notes some publications use the S in IMSAFE for both stress and emotion and the E for eating, since nutrition and hydration matter [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Either version covers K2d.

You are not expected to be a psychologist [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Keep notes of what you saw, factually, so the unbiased instructor and you can confer [[25:49|AIH 2-16]]. Application: write behavior, not diagnoses.
Praise is powerful but loses value when given too freely [[25:162|AIH 8-4]]. Make it specific to a real milestone, such as performance reaching the ACS standard [[25:37|AIH 2-4]].
gaps: The AIH and PHAK give no amount of water to drink per flight hour; the PHAK gives only a daily guide of two to four quarts [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
No source gives a form or wording for the learner questionnaire beyond sample questions [[25:37|AIH 2-4]]. Build your own.
The AIH says to recommend a professional counselor in severe cases [[25:45|AIH 2-12]] but names no referral process or FAA reporting channel. Ask your school or an Aviation Medical Examiner.
The AIH does not say which personality type test to use, and notes the idea of teaching by personality type is controversial [[25:34|AIH 2-1]].
No source says how many minutes of discomfort or illness should end a lesson; the AIH leaves it to the instructor, except that airsickness ends the flight as soon as it starts [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

activities.title: Dehydration numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: The PHAK guide is eight glasses of water a day at 8 ounces each. How many ounces is that?
items.why: 8 x 8 = 64 ounces, which the PHAK says equals two quarts [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

items.q: The PHAK guide tops out at four quarts per 24 hours. If two quarts are 64 ounces, how many ounces are four quarts?
Most people get thirsty after losing 2 percent of body weight. For a 180-pound learner, how many pounds is that?
items.why: 0.02 x 180 = 3.6 pounds [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. The thirst mechanism arrives too late, so drink before you feel it.

items.q: The other thirst trigger the PHAK gives is a 1.5-quart deficit. How many ounces is that, at 32 ounces per quart?
items.why: 1.5 x 32 = 48 ounces, using 64 ounces = two quarts [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

items.q: By the preflight briefing your learner has had three 8-ounce glasses of water today. How many more ounces does she need to reach the low end of the PHAK guide (two quarts)?
items.why: Two quarts = 64 ounces [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. 64 - 3 x 8 = 64 - 24 = 40 ounces. The PHAK says this is only a guide, since each person is different [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

activities.title: True or false: adults and emotions
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Adults are ready to learn when they take on new roles, such as a new job.
cards.why: True. Adults seek learning to cope with life-changing events and are ready when they assume new roles [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

cards.s: Because adults are self-directed, the instructor should leave them to learn alone.
cards.why: False. Self-direction does not mean isolation; self-directed projects use other people as resources and guides [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

cards.s: An instructor is responsible for meeting every expectation the learner brings.
cards.why: False. The instructor assumes responsibility only for their own expectations and should clarify the learner's early [[25:50|AIH 2-17]].

cards.s: Worries and upsets caused by the training course are often due to shortcomings of the course or the instructor.
cards.why: True. The AIH says these problems are often due to inadequacies of the course or the instructor, and prevention is the best cure [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

cards.s: Some people react to anxiety more rapidly and adequately than they would without the threat.
cards.why: True. Some react appropriately and faster under threat, while many freeze [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

cards.s: Chronic fatigue is always cured by a good night's sleep.
cards.why: False. Chronic fatigue may have deeper roots, so rest alone may not resolve it [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

activities.title: A tense lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for Dana, a 38-year-old learner with 15 hours, in a two-seat trainer on a hot afternoon.

steps.s: Dana arrives after an afternoon of yard work in the heat, has had no water, and says she feels a little light-headed.
options: Fly but skip the preflight to save energy
Get her water and shorten or postpone the flight lesson
Fly the full lesson as planned
Fly and do the hardest maneuvers first while she is fresh
steps.why: Dehydration reduces alertness and slows decisions, and its first effect is fatigue [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Fatigue is the primary consideration in lesson length [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

steps.s: A week later she is quiet and distracted before a steep turn lesson. She mentions her company is laying people off.
options: Tell her outside problems are not part of flight training and press on
Stop her training until her job is secure
Add harder maneuvers to take her mind off it
Acknowledge it, then key the lesson to her interests and steer her attention to the task at hand
steps.why: Outside troubles affect learning and cannot be ignored, though you are not responsible for them; key instruction to the interests she brings and divert her attention from her worries to the task [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

steps.s: In the debrief she says her sloppy steep turns were your fault for "rushing the briefing."
options: Report her to the chief instructor
Argue the point until she admits it
Recognize possible projection, discuss the facts calmly and aim to rebuild her confidence
Agree and say nothing more
steps.why: Blaming someone else for a shortcoming is projection [[25:43|AIH 2-10]]. Discuss it with common sense and aim to restore motivation and self-confidence [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. If the briefing really was rushed, admit it [[25:162|AIH 8-4]].

steps.s: Next lesson, you want to check she understood the steep turn roll-out.
options: "Walk me through how you will roll out on your entry heading."
"Do you know the recovery, yes or no?"
"Who, what, when, where and why of steep turns?"
"Got it?"
steps.why: Ask a focused, open-ended question on one idea; an open-ended question can be a statement that asks for completion [[25:103|AIH 4-10]].

steps.s: On short final she gets low and you need her to act now.
options: "Do something about that."
"Go around."
"Take appropriate measures."
Explain the glidepath in detail
steps.why: Use concrete words with one meaning; "go around" works where "take appropriate measures" may not [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].
